practice.prompt: Use your calculator to find sec 10°, correct to two decimal places.
practice.why: Learners forget the 1 over and just write cos 10° = 0,98.
practice.rightWay: Write sec 10° as 1/cos 10° and press 1 ÷ ( cos 10° ) in degrees mode. The answer is 1,02.

practice.prompt: Use your calculator to find cot 32°, correct to two decimal places.
practice.why: Learners sometimes use cos or sin instead of tan for cot.
practice.rightWay: Cot is 1/tan, so press 1 ÷ ( tan 32° ) in degrees mode. The answer is 1,60.

practice.prompt: Use your calculator to find cosec 25°, correct to two decimal places.
practice.why: Learners give sin 25° = 0,42 instead of taking the reciprocal.
practice.rightWay: Cosec is 1/sin, so press 1 ÷ ( sin 25° ) in degrees mode. The answer is 2,37.

practice.prompt: Use your calculator to find sec 48°, correct to two decimal places.
practice.why: Learners forget to divide 1 by the cosine value and give 0,67.
practice.rightWay: Sec is 1/cos, so press 1 ÷ ( cos 48° ) in degrees mode. The answer is 1,49.

practice.prompt: Which statement is correct?
steps: sec θ is the reciprocal of cos θ
practice.why: Learners mix up which reciprocal belongs to which ratio.
practice.rightWay: Sec is the reciprocal of cos, so sec θ = 1/cos θ. Cosec goes with sin and cot goes with tan.

practice.prompt: Use your calculator to find 2 sec 25°, correct to two decimal places.
practice.why: Learners multiply 2 by cos 25° instead of 2 by the reciprocal of cos 25°.
practice.rightWay: First find sec 25° = 1/cos 25° = 1,1034..., then multiply by 2. The answer is 2,21.

practice.prompt: Use your calculator to find cot 35° + cosec 40°, correct to two decimal places.
practice.why: Learners convert only one of the two reciprocal ratios and mix sin with tan.
practice.rightWay: Convert both ratios: cot 35° is 1/tan 35° and cosec 40° is 1/sin 40°. Add the two decimal values. The answer is about 2,98.

lessons.title: Special angles without a calculator
objectives: You will be able to build the 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 triangles from simple side lengths.
You will be able to state the exact values of sin, cos and tan for 30, 45 and 60 degrees.
You will be able to simplify expressions using these exact values.

keyWords.meaning: The angles 30 degrees, 45 degrees and 60 degrees, whose sin, cos and tan values are exact simple numbers.
A value written as a fraction or surd (like 1/2 or sqrt(3)), not a rounded decimal from a calculator.
A root like sqrt(2) or sqrt(3) left in root form instead of worked out as a decimal.
A triangle with two equal sides; the angles opposite the equal sides are also equal.
Rewrite a fraction so there is no root in the denominator, for example 1/sqrt(2) becomes sqrt(2)/2.

blocks.text:
In earlier lessons you found sin, cos and tan of angles using a calculator, which gives decimals like 0,7071. But some angles give beautifully simple exact answers, and a calculator is not needed at all.

These are the special angles: 30 degrees, 45 degrees and 60 degrees. Their values come from two simple triangles, and exam questions often ask you to work with the exact values rather than decimals.
blocks.speech: In earlier lessons you used a calculator to find sin, cos and tan. But for three special angles, thirty degrees, forty-five degrees and sixty degrees, the values are exact simple numbers. In this lesson you will build the two triangles that give these values, and use them without a calculator.

blocks.text:
Start with a square of side 1 and cut it along a diagonal. You get two right-angled triangles with angles 45, 45 and 90 degrees, because the diagonal cuts each 90 degree corner in half.

The two legs are both 1. By Pythagoras the hypotenuse is sqrt(1^2 + 1^2) = sqrt(2). So the 45-45-90 triangle has sides 1, 1 and sqrt(2).
blocks.speech: Take a square with sides of length one, and cut it along a diagonal. You get a right-angled triangle with angles forty-five, forty-five and ninety degrees. The two shorter sides are both one, and by the theorem of Pythagoras the hypotenuse is the square root of two.

blocks.caption: The 45-45-90 triangle: legs 1 and 1, hypotenuse sqrt(2)
blocks.speech: The picture shows a right-angled triangle. The angle at A is forty-five degrees, the angle at B is forty-five degrees, and the right angle is at C. The two legs are each of length one, and the hypotenuse is the square root of two.

blocks.problem: Use the 45-45-90 triangle to find the exact values of sin 45 degrees, cos 45 degrees and tan 45 degrees.

steps.line: From the angle 45 degrees: opposite = 1, adjacent = 1, hypotenuse = sqrt(2)
steps.reason: Label the sides with respect to either 45 degree angle; the triangle is isosceles so both legs are 1.
Sine is opposite over hypotenuse.
Cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse; the sides are equal so the ratios match.
Tangent is opposite over adjacent, and one divided by one is one.

blocks.speech: We use the forty-five forty-five ninety triangle. Relative to a forty-five degree angle, the opposite side is one, the adjacent side is one, and the hypotenuse is the square root of two. So sin forty-five degrees is one over root two, cos forty-five degrees is also one over root two, and tan forty-five degrees is one over one, which is one.

blocks.text:
Now build the 30-60-90 triangle. Take an equilateral triangle with all sides 2 and cut it down the middle. Each half is a right-angled triangle with angles 30, 60 and 90 degrees.

The base is split into two halves of 1, the vertical height is sqrt(2^2 - 1^2) = sqrt(3), and the hypotenuse stays 2. So the 30-60-90 triangle has sides 1, sqrt(3) and 2, with the side of length 1 opposite the 30 degree angle.
blocks.speech: Now build the thirty sixty ninety triangle. Cut an equilateral triangle with sides two down the middle. Each half has a base of one, a height of root three by Pythagoras, and a hypotenuse of two. The side of length one is opposite the thirty degree angle.

blocks.caption: The 30-60-90 triangle: sides 1, sqrt(3) and 2
blocks.speech: The picture shows a right-angled triangle with the angle at A equal to thirty degrees, the angle at B equal to sixty degrees, and the right angle at C. The short side opposite the thirty degree angle is one, the side opposite the sixty degree angle is root three, and the hypotenuse is two.

blocks.problem: Use the 30-60-90 triangle to find the exact values of sin 30 degrees, cos 30 degrees and tan 30 degrees.

steps.line: From the 30 degree angle: opposite = 1, adjacent = sqrt(3), hypotenuse = 2
steps.reason: The side of length 1 is opposite the 30 degree angle; the other leg is next to the 30 degree angle.
Sine is opposite over hypotenuse: 1 over 2.
Cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse: sqrt(3) over 2.
Tangent is opposite over adjacent: 1 over sqrt(3).

blocks.speech: Relative to the thirty degree angle, the opposite side is one, the adjacent side is root three, and the hypotenuse is two. So sin thirty degrees is one over two, cos thirty degrees is root three over two, and tan thirty degrees is one over root three.

blocks.text:
For the 60 degree angle in the same triangle the sides swap roles: the opposite side becomes sqrt(3) and the adjacent side becomes 1.

sin 60° = sqrt(3)/2, cos 60° = 1/2, tan 60° = sqrt(3).

Here is the full table to memorise. For 45 degrees: sin = 1/sqrt(2), cos = 1/sqrt(2), tan = 1. For 30 degrees: sin = 1/2, cos = sqrt(3)/2, tan = 1/sqrt(3). For 60 degrees: sin = sqrt(3)/2, cos = 1/2, tan = sqrt(3). Notice sin 30 = cos 60 and cos 30 = sin 60; the values swap.
blocks.speech: For the sixty degree angle in the same triangle the opposite and adjacent sides swap. Sin sixty is root three over two, cos sixty is one over two, and tan sixty is root three. Memorise the table: sin thirty is a half, sin forty-five is one over root two, sin sixty is root three over two, and cos thirty is root three over two, cos forty-five is one over root two, cos sixty is a half. Tan thirty is one over root three, tan forty-five is one, tan sixty is root three.

blocks.problem: Calculate sin 45 degrees times cos 45 degrees without a calculator.

steps.reason: Replace each ratio with its exact special-angle value.
Multiply the fractions: multiply numerators and denominators.
sqrt(2) times sqrt(2) is exactly 2.

blocks.speech: Sin forty-five times cos forty-five. Replace each value: one over root two times one over root two. Multiply the fractions to get one over root two times root two, and root two times root two is two. So the answer is one half.

blocks.problem: Calculate cos 60 degrees + tan 45 degrees without a calculator.

steps.reason: Use the exact values: cos 60 degrees is 1/2 and tan 45 degrees is 1.
Write 1 as 2/2 so the fractions have the same denominator.
Add the numerators over the common denominator 2.

blocks.speech: Cos sixty plus tan forty-five. Cos sixty is a half and tan forty-five is one. Add: a half plus two halves is three halves.

blocks.problem: Calculate tan 30 degrees minus sin 60 degrees without a calculator. Leave your answer in surd form.

steps.reason: Replace each ratio with its exact special-angle value.
Write both fractions over the common denominator 2sqrt(3).
sqrt(3) times sqrt(3) is 3, so the second numerator is 3.
Two minus three is minus one.

blocks.speech: Tan thirty minus sin sixty. Replace: one over root three minus root three over two. Put both over the common denominator two root three. The first numerator is two, and root three times root three is three, so the second numerator is three. Two minus three is minus one, so the answer is minus one over two root three.

question.prompt: Calculate tan 45 degrees ÷ sin 60 degrees without a calculator. Give the exact value.
question.why: Learners often divide by the fraction incorrectly instead of multiplying by its reciprocal.
question.rightWay: Write tan 45 degrees as 1, then dividing by sqrt(3)/2 means multiplying by 2/sqrt(3), which gives 2/sqrt(3).

blocks.hint: Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal.
blocks.speech: Try this: tan forty-five degrees divided by sin sixty degrees. Tan forty-five degrees is one, and sin sixty degrees is root three over two. Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its upside-down fraction.

blocks.why: The side of length 1 is opposite the 30 degree angle, and sqrt(3) is adjacent to the 30 degree angle. The short side goes with the small angle, so sin 30 degrees is 1/2 and it is cos 30 degrees that equals sqrt(3)/2.
blocks.speech: A common mistake is saying sin thirty degrees is root three over two. The short side of length one is opposite the thirty degree angle, so sin thirty degrees is one half. It is cos thirty degrees that equals root three over two. Remember: the smallest angle faces the shortest side.

blocks.text:
To simplify any expression with special angles, follow three steps. First, replace every ratio with its exact value from the table. Second, work out the arithmetic, writing fractions over a common denominator when needed. Third, leave roots like sqrt(3) in your answer; do not convert to decimals unless the question says so.

With practice you can also show that identities like sin^2 45 degrees + cos^2 45 degrees = 1 are true, by substituting the exact values on both sides.
blocks.speech: To simplify any expression, replace each ratio with its exact value, work out the arithmetic with common denominators, and leave the roots in surd form. You can even prove identities this way, for example sin squared forty-five plus cos squared forty-five is one half plus one half, which is one.

summary: sin 45° = cos 45° = 1/sqrt(2) and tan 45° = 1, from the isosceles triangle with sides 1, 1, sqrt(2).
sin 30° = cos 60° = 1/2, cos 30° = sin 60° = sqrt(3)/2, tan 30° = 1/sqrt(3), tan 60° = sqrt(3).
The values come from the 30-60-90 triangle with sides 1, sqrt(3) and 2.
To simplify an expression, replace each ratio by its exact value and simplify, keeping surds in the answer.
The small angle faces the short side: sin 30° = 1/2, not sqrt(3)/2.

practice.prompt: Write down the exact value of cos 60 degrees.
steps: From the 30-60-90 triangle: adjacent to 60 degrees is 1, hypotenuse is 2
practice.why: Learners mix up cos 60 degrees with cos 30 degrees.
practice.rightWay: In the 30-60-90 triangle the side next to the 60 degree angle is 1 and the hypotenuse is 2, so cos 60 degrees is 1/2.

practice.prompt: Write down the exact value of tan 45 degrees.
practice.why: Learners sometimes guess a surd instead of noticing the two legs are equal.
practice.rightWay: In the 45-45-90 triangle the opposite and adjacent sides are both 1, so tan 45 degrees is 1.

practice.prompt: Write down the exact value of sin 60 degrees.
steps: In the 30-60-90 triangle: opposite the 60 degree angle is sqrt(3), hypotenuse is 2
practice.why: Learners swap the values of sin 30 degrees and sin 60 degrees.
practice.rightWay: The side opposite the 60 degree angle is sqrt(3) and the hypotenuse is 2, so sin 60 degrees is sqrt(3)/2.

practice.prompt: Calculate sin 45 degrees × cos 45 degrees without a calculator.
practice.why: Learners multiply roots incorrectly and write sqrt(4) instead of realising sqrt(2) × sqrt(2) = 2.
practice.rightWay: Replace each ratio with 1/sqrt(2), multiply the fractions, and use sqrt(2) × sqrt(2) = 2 to get 1/2.

practice.prompt: Calculate cos 60 degrees + tan 45 degrees without a calculator.
practice.why: Learners forget that tan 45 degrees is 1 and add wrong values.
practice.rightWay: Cos 60 degrees is 1/2 and tan 45 degrees is 1; writing 1 as 2/2 gives the sum 3/2.

practice.prompt: Calculate tan 30 degrees - sin 60 degrees without a calculator, in surd form.
practice.why: Learners use a wrong common denominator or forget that sqrt(3) × sqrt(3) = 3.
practice.rightWay: Put both fractions over the common denominator 2sqrt(3); the numerators are 2 and 3, giving minus 1 over 2sqrt(3).

practice.prompt: Calculate sin 60 degrees - cos 60 degrees without a calculator, in surd form.
practice.why: Learners try to subtract 1/2 from sqrt(3)/2 as if sqrt(3) were a number like 3.
practice.rightWay: Both fractions have denominator 2, so subtract the numerators: sqrt(3)/2 minus 1/2 is (sqrt(3) - 1)/2.

practice.prompt: Which statement about tan x is true for angles between 0 and 90 degrees?
steps: The opposite and adjacent sides can take any values, so the ratio is not limited by the hypotenuse
So tan x has no maximum value
choices: tan x has a maximum value of 1
tan x has a maximum value of 2
tan x has no maximum value
practice.why: Learners assume all trig ratios are at most 1, but tangent compares the two shorter sides, not a side with the hypotenuse.
practice.rightWay: Sine and cosine have one side over the hypotenuse, so they are at most 1. Tangent is opposite over adjacent, and those sides can grow, so tan has no maximum.

lessons.title: Finding a missing side
objectives: You will be able to choose sin, cos or tan from the angle and the two sides involved.
You will be able to set up an equation with the unknown side and solve it.
You will be able to round the answer sensibly and check that the side length is reasonable.

keyWords.meaning: The longest side of a right-angled triangle, always opposite the right angle.
The side directly across from the angle you are working with.
The side next to the angle you are working with, that is not the hypotenuse.
A comparison of two lengths by division, like opposite over hypotenuse.
A maths sentence with an equals sign that you can solve for an unknown.
Writing a decimal answer to a given number of decimal places, like 76,60.

blocks.text:
So far you have named the sides of a right-angled triangle and used the ratios sin, cos and tan. Now we put that to work: if you know one angle and one side of a right-angled triangle, you can calculate any other side. This is the whole point of trigonometry for many exam questions.

The plan is always the same: label the sides, choose the ratio that uses the two sides you care about, write an equation, and solve it.
blocks.speech: In this lesson we learn how to find a missing side of a right-angled triangle. If you know one angle and one side, trigonometry lets you work out the others. The plan is always the same: label the sides, choose the right ratio, write an equation, and solve it.

blocks.caption: Right-angled triangle ABC: the right angle is at C, the angle at A is 50°, the hypotenuse is 100 and the side opposite the 50° angle is marked x.
blocks.speech: Look at the triangle. The right angle is at C. The angle at A is fifty degrees. The hypotenuse, opposite the right angle, is one hundred. The side opposite the fifty degree angle is x, and that is what we want to find.

blocks.text:
To choose the correct ratio, look at the angle given and ask: which two sides are involved? The side you know, and the side you want.

If they are opposite and hypotenuse, use sin. If they are adjacent and hypotenuse, use cos. If they are opposite and adjacent, use tan. The known side and the unknown side decide the ratio, never guess.

SOH CAH TOA from the earlier lesson is your checklist: Sin = Opposite/Hypotenuse, Cos = Adjacent/Hypotenuse, Tan = Opposite/Adjacent.
blocks.speech: To choose the ratio, look at the angle and ask which two sides are involved. Opposite and hypotenuse means use sine. Adjacent and hypotenuse means use cosine. Opposite and adjacent means use tangent. Soh cah toa is your checklist.

blocks.problem: Find the length of x in the triangle with the right angle at C, the angle at A equal to 50°, the hypotenuse equal to 100 and x opposite the 50° angle. Round to 2 decimal places.

steps.reason: x is opposite the angle and 100 is the hypotenuse, so use sin = opposite/hypotenuse
multiply both sides by 100 to get x on its own
rewrite with x on the left, the way exam markers like it
use the calculator in degree mode to find sin 50°
round to two decimal places

blocks.speech: We want x, which is opposite the fifty degree angle, and the hypotenuse is one hundred. So we use sine. Sine fifty equals x over one hundred. Multiply both sides by one hundred, so x equals one hundred times sine fifty. The calculator gives zero point seven six six, times one hundred is seventy six point six zero. So x is about seventy six, six zero units.

blocks.text:
When the unknown side is in the denominator (the bottom of the fraction), you need an extra step: multiply both sides by the unknown first, then divide by the trig value.

A quick rule that always works: get the unknown alone. If x is on top, multiply by the known side. If x is at the bottom, divide by the trig value at the end.

Also check your answer makes sense: the hypotenuse must be the longest side, so any side you find must be shorter than the hypotenuse.
blocks.speech: When the unknown side is at the bottom of the fraction, multiply both sides by it first, then divide by the trig value at the end. Always check: the hypotenuse is the longest side, so your answer must be shorter than the hypotenuse.

blocks.problem: Find the length of x in the right-angled triangle where the angle is 25°, the side adjacent to the angle is 7 and x is the hypotenuse. Round to 2 decimal places.

steps.reason: 7 is adjacent to the angle and x is the hypotenuse, so use cos = adjacent/hypotenuse
multiply both sides by x to move x out of the denominator
divide both sides by cos 25° to get x alone
use the calculator to find cos 25°
divide and round to two decimal places

blocks.speech: Here the adjacent side is seven and the hypotenuse is x, so we use cosine. Cosine twenty five equals seven over x. Multiply both sides by x: x cosine twenty five equals seven. Divide both sides by cosine twenty five: x equals seven over cosine twenty five. That is seven divided by zero point nine zero six, which is seven point seven two. The hypotenuse is the longest side and seven point seven two is longer than seven, so it checks out.

question.prompt: In a right-angled triangle the angle is 37°, the hypotenuse is 62 and a is the side opposite the 37° angle. Find a correct to 2 decimal places.
question.why: Learners often use cos instead of sin, or forget that a is on top so they must multiply by 62.
question.rightWay: a is opposite and 62 is the hypotenuse, so sin 37° = a/62, so a = 62 sin 37° = 37,31.

blocks.hint: The side a is opposite the angle and 62 is the hypotenuse. Which ratio uses those two sides?
blocks.speech: Try this one. The angle is thirty seven degrees, the hypotenuse is sixty two, and a is the opposite side. Write the sine ratio, solve for a by multiplying by sixty two, and round to two decimal places.

blocks.why: When the unknown is in the denominator, multiplying by the trig value makes it smaller instead of solving for x. You must divide by cos 25° to free the x.
blocks.speech: Here is a common mistake. For cos twenty five equals seven over x, some learners write x equals seven times cosine twenty five, giving six point three four. That is wrong. The right way is x equals seven divided by cosine twenty five, which is seven point seven two. Multiplying makes the number smaller, but the hypotenuse must be longer than the adjacent side, so dividing is the only sensible answer.

blocks.text:
The tangent ratio handles the case where the two sides involved are the opposite and the adjacent, with no hypotenuse at all.

If you know the adjacent side and want the opposite side, x is on top: tan θ = x/(known side), so x = known side × tan θ.

If you know the opposite side and want the adjacent side, x is at the bottom: tan θ = known side/x, so x = known side ÷ tan θ.
blocks.speech: Tangent handles the case with opposite and adjacent sides. If the unknown is on top, multiply by the known side times tan of the angle. If the unknown is at the bottom, divide the known side by tan of the angle.

blocks.problem: In a right-angled triangle the angle is 55°, the side opposite the angle is 4,1 and x is the adjacent side. Find x correct to 2 decimal places.

steps.reason: 4,1 is opposite the angle and x is adjacent, so use tan = opposite/adjacent
multiply both sides by x to move x out of the denominator
divide both sides by tan 55°
use the calculator to find tan 55°
divide and round to two decimal places

blocks.speech: The opposite side is four point one and the adjacent side is x, so we use tangent. Tan fifty five equals four point one over x. Multiply both sides by x, then divide both sides by tan fifty five. x equals four point one divided by one point four two eight, which is two point eight seven.

question.prompt: In a right-angled triangle the angle is 49°, the hypotenuse is 33 and d is the side adjacent to the 49° angle. Find d correct to 2 decimal places.
question.why: Using sin instead of cos, or writing cos 49° = 33/d instead of d/33, are the usual errors here.
question.rightWay: d is adjacent and 33 is the hypotenuse, so cos 49° = d/33, so d = 33 cos 49° = 21,65.

blocks.hint: d is adjacent to the angle and 33 is the hypotenuse, so the cosine ratio applies, and d is on top of the fraction.
blocks.speech: Try this. The angle is forty nine degrees, the hypotenuse is thirty three, and d is the adjacent side. Cosine forty nine equals d over thirty three. Multiply by thirty three to find d, and round to two decimal places.

blocks.text:
Exam questions often hide the triangle inside a story: a ladder against a wall, a kite on a string, a ramp. First draw the right-angled triangle yourself and mark the angle and the two sides. Then use exactly the same steps.

Before you write your final answer, ask: is this length sensible? The hypotenuse must be the longest side. An opposite side is longer than the adjacent side only when the angle is bigger than 45°. A quick sketch check catches most slips.
blocks.speech: Exam questions often hide the triangle in a story about a ladder or a kite. Draw the right-angled triangle first, mark the angle and sides, then use the same steps. Always check the answer is sensible: the hypotenuse is the longest side.

blocks.problem: A kite string is 50 m long and makes an angle of 40° with the ground. How high is the kite above the ground? Round to 2 decimal places.

steps.line: Draw the triangle: the string is the hypotenuse, the height h is opposite the 40° angle
steps.reason: the height rises straight up from the ground, so the triangle is right-angled
h is opposite and 50 is the hypotenuse, so use sin = opposite/hypotenuse
multiply both sides by 50
use the calculator to find sin 40°
round to two decimal places

blocks.speech: A kite string is fifty metres long at forty degrees to the ground. Draw the triangle: the string is the hypotenuse and the height h is opposite the angle. So sine forty equals h over fifty. Multiply by fifty: h equals fifty times sine forty, which is fifty times zero point six four three, about thirty two point one four metres. That is less than the string length, so it is sensible.

question.prompt: In a right-angled triangle the angle is 30°, the hypotenuse is 20 and h is the side opposite the 30° angle. Find h.
question.why: Learners sometimes forget that sin 30° is exactly one half and reach for the calculator unnecessarily, or round 10 to 10,00 and type it wrongly.
question.rightWay: h is opposite and 20 is the hypotenuse, so sin 30° = h/20, so h = 20 × 0,5 = 10.

blocks.hint: sin 30° is one of the special angles from the earlier lesson: it equals exactly 1/2.
blocks.speech: Last try. The angle is thirty degrees, the hypotenuse is twenty, and h is opposite. Sine thirty is one half, so h equals twenty times one half. What is h?

blocks.text: Every missing-side question follows the same four steps. One: mark the given angle and label opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse. Two: choose the ratio from the two sides involved. Three: write the equation and solve, multiplying by the known side if the unknown is on top, dividing by the trig value if it is at the bottom. Four: round to 2 decimal places and check the side is sensible. Practise until this is automatic, because the next lesson uses the same steps to find a missing angle.
blocks.speech: To sum up the method. One: label the sides. Two: choose sine, cosine or tangent from the two sides involved. Three: write the equation and solve for the unknown. Four: round to two decimal places and check the answer is sensible. Next lesson we use the same ideas to find a missing angle.

summary: Label opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse with respect to the given angle.
Opposite and hypotenuse: use sin. Adjacent and hypotenuse: use cos. Opposite and adjacent: use tan.
If the unknown is on top: x = known side × trig value. If it is at the bottom: x = known side ÷ trig value.
Round to 2 decimal places and check: the hypotenuse must be the longest side.

practice.prompt: In a right-angled triangle the angle is 30°, the hypotenuse is 20 and h is the side opposite the 30° angle. Find h.
practice.why: Forgetting that sin 30° is exactly 1/2 leads to unnecessary calculator work and rounding slips.
practice.rightWay: h is opposite and 20 is the hypotenuse, so h = 20 sin 30° = 10.

practice.prompt: In a right-angled triangle the angle is 55°, the hypotenuse is 19 and c is the side adjacent to the 55° angle. Find c correct to 2 decimal places.
practice.why: Using sin instead of cos swaps the opposite and adjacent sides and gives the wrong answer.
practice.rightWay: c is adjacent and 19 is the hypotenuse, so c = 19 cos 55° = 10,90.

practice.prompt: In a right-angled triangle the angle is 23°, the adjacent side is 21 and b is the side opposite the 23° angle. Find b correct to 2 decimal places.
practice.why: Learners often use sin or cos here, but neither hypotenuse is involved, so tan is the only correct ratio.
practice.rightWay: b is opposite and 21 is adjacent, so b = 21 tan 23° = 8,91.

practice.prompt: In a right-angled triangle the angle is 17°, the side opposite is 12 and e is the hypotenuse. Find e correct to 2 decimal places.
practice.why: When the unknown hypotenuse is at the bottom, learners multiply instead of divide and get a value smaller than 12.
practice.rightWay: 12 is opposite and e is the hypotenuse, so e = 12/sin 17° = 41,04.

practice.prompt: In a right-angled triangle the angle is 22°, the side adjacent is 31 and f is the hypotenuse. Find f correct to 2 decimal places.
practice.why: Writing cos 22° = f/31 puts the known and unknown sides in the wrong places in the fraction.
practice.rightWay: 31 is adjacent and f is the hypotenuse, so f = 31/cos 22° = 33,43.

practice.prompt: A ladder leans against a wall at 65° to the flat ground. The foot of the ladder is 4,23 m from the wall. How high up the wall does the ladder reach? Round to 2 decimal places.
practice.why: Drawing the angle at the wrong place in the sketch mixes up opposite and adjacent, so the wrong ratio gets used.
practice.rightWay: The height is opposite the 65° angle and 4,23 is adjacent, so h = 4,23 tan 65° = 9,07 m.

practice.prompt: In triangle MNP, angle N is 90°, MP = 20 and angle P is 40°. Calculate MN, the side opposite angle P, correct to 2 decimal places.
practice.why: MP is the hypotenuse because it is opposite the right angle at N; treating it as an adjacent side gives the wrong ratio.
practice.rightWay: Angle N is 90°, so MP is the hypotenuse and MN is opposite angle P: MN = 20 sin 40° = 12,86.

lessons.title: Finding a missing angle and simple equations
objectives: You will be able to use inverse sin, cos and tan to find an unknown angle in a right-angled triangle.
You will be able to solve simple equations such as 2 sin theta = 1 or tan theta = 0.5.
You will be able to decide whether an answer should be an exact special angle or a calculator angle.

keyWords.meaning: The side across from the angle you are working with in a right-angled triangle.
The side next to the angle you are working with, which is not the hypotenuse.
The longest side of a right-angled triangle, always across from the right angle.
sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹: it works backwards from a ratio to give the angle.
One of the angles 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90° whose ratios are known without a calculator.
An answer like 30° that comes from a special angle and needs no rounding.
What you write when sin or cos of an angle would have to be more than 1.

blocks.text:
Last lesson you were given an angle and used a trig ratio to find a missing side. Today the problem is turned around: two sides of a right-angled triangle are known, and the angle is unknown.

Because the ratio of two sides fixes the angle completely, trigonometry can find it. This is how engineers set the slope of a ramp, how surveyors measure angles they cannot walk to, and how GPS pinpoints your position.
blocks.speech: In the last lesson you knew an angle and used a trig ratio to find a missing side. Today we turn the problem around. Now two sides of a right-angled triangle are known, and the angle is the unknown. Because the ratio of two sides fixes the angle completely, trigonometry can find it. Engineers use this to set the slope of a ramp, surveyors use it to measure angles they cannot walk to, and the GPS in a phone uses it to work out your position.

blocks.caption: Name the sides from the angle θ: opposite is across from θ, adjacent is next to θ, hypotenuse is across from the right angle.
blocks.speech: The picture shows a right-angled triangle with the right angle at B. The side across from the angle theta is called the opposite side. The side next to theta, the one that is not the hypotenuse, is called the adjacent side. The longest side, across from the right angle, is always the hypotenuse. Which two sides you know decides whether you use sine, cosine or tangent.

blocks.text:
If sin 30° = 0,5, then 30° is the angle whose sine is 0,5. The inverse function asks the question backwards: sin⁻¹(0,5) = 30°. Read sin⁻¹ as 'the angle whose sine is'.

On most calculators the inverse functions sit above sin, cos and tan, behind the SHIFT or 2nd F key. Careful: sin⁻¹ does not mean 1 divided by sin.
blocks.speech: If sine of thirty degrees equals zero point five, then thirty degrees is the angle whose sine is zero point five. The inverse function asks the question backwards: inverse sine of zero point five gives thirty degrees. Say it as the angle whose sine is. On most calculators the inverse functions are above the sine, cosine and tangent keys, behind the shift or second function key. And a warning: inverse sine does not mean one divided by sine; it means go back from the ratio to the angle.

blocks.problem: In a right-angled triangle, the side opposite θ is 1 and the hypotenuse is 2. Find θ.

steps.reason: The opposite side and hypotenuse are known, so use the sine ratio.
Simplify the fraction to a decimal.
Apply the inverse sine to go back from the ratio to the angle.
0,5 is the exact sine of the special angle 30°, so the answer is exact.

blocks.speech: Worked example one. In a right-angled triangle, the side opposite theta is one and the hypotenuse is two. Find theta. The opposite and hypotenuse are known, so use the sine ratio. Sine theta equals one over two, which is zero point five. Apply inverse sine to both sides: theta equals inverse sine of zero point five. That is the special angle thirty degrees, an exact answer. The diagram shows the triangle with the right angle at B, the side of one opposite theta, and the hypotenuse of two.

blocks.caption: The 30°-60°-90° triangle. If your ratio matches one of these values, the angle is exact.
blocks.speech: This is the thirty, sixty, ninety triangle from Lesson four. The side opposite thirty degrees is one, the side opposite sixty degrees is the square root of three, and the hypotenuse is two. So sine of thirty degrees is one half, cosine of sixty degrees is one half, tangent of sixty degrees is the square root of three, and tangent of thirty degrees is one over the square root of three. When the ratio in your equation matches one of these values, you can write the angle exactly, with no calculator and no rounding.

blocks.problem: In a right-angled triangle, the side opposite θ is 4 and the side adjacent to θ is 9. Find θ, correct to 2 decimal places.

steps.reason: The opposite and adjacent sides are known, so use the tangent ratio.
Work out the ratio as a decimal.
Apply the inverse tangent to go back from the ratio to the angle.
The calculator works out the inverse tangent.
Round to 2 decimal places as the question asks.

blocks.speech: Worked example two. In a right-angled triangle the side opposite theta is four and the side adjacent to theta is nine. Find theta, correct to two decimal places. The opposite and adjacent sides are known, so use tangent. Tan theta equals four ninths, which is zero point four four four and so on. Apply inverse tangent: theta equals inverse tan of four ninths. The calculator gives twenty-three point nine six two four degrees, which rounds to twenty-three point nine six degrees. This time the answer is not exact, so we round as the question asks.

blocks.text:
An equation like 2 sin θ = 1 or tan θ = 0,5 is solved the same way. First use ordinary algebra to get the sin, cos or tan completely alone: divide both sides, add or subtract as needed. Only then apply the inverse function.

If the ratio is a clean special value like 0,5 or 1, the answer is exact. Otherwise give the calculator angle, rounded as the question asks.
blocks.speech: An equation like two sin theta equals one, or tan theta equals zero point five, is solved the same way. First use ordinary algebra to get the sine, cosine or tangent completely alone. Divide both sides by two, or add or subtract as needed. Only then apply the inverse function. If the ratio is a clean special value like zero point five or one, the answer is an exact angle. Otherwise give the calculator angle, rounded the way the question asks.

blocks.problem: Solve for θ: 4 cos θ = 2.

steps.reason: The given equation.
Divide both sides by 4 to get cos θ alone.
Apply the inverse cosine to go back from the ratio to the angle.
0,5 is the exact cosine of the special angle 60°, so the answer is exact.

blocks.speech: Worked example three. Solve for theta: four cos theta equals two. Divide both sides by four to get cos theta alone: cos theta equals two over four, which is zero point five. Apply inverse cosine: theta equals inverse cos of zero point five. Zero point five is the cosine of sixty degrees, so theta equals sixty degrees, an exact answer. No rounding needed.

blocks.problem: A 5 m ladder leans against a wall. Its foot is 3 m from the wall. Find the angle the ladder makes with the ground, correct to 2 decimal places.

steps.line: Hypotenuse = 5 m (the ladder), adjacent = 3 m (the ground)
steps.reason: Identify the sides: the ladder is across from the right angle, so it is the hypotenuse.
Adjacent and hypotenuse are known, so use the cosine ratio.
Simplify the fraction.
Apply the inverse cosine.
The calculator works out the angle.
Round to 2 decimal places.

blocks.speech: Worked example four. A five metre ladder leans against a wall, and its foot is three metres from the wall. Find the angle the ladder makes with the ground, correct to two decimal places. The ladder is the hypotenuse, five metres. The ground side next to the angle is the adjacent side, three metres. Adjacent over hypotenuse is the cosine ratio. Cos theta equals three over five, which is zero point six. Theta equals inverse cos of zero point six. The calculator gives fifty-three point one three zero one degrees, so theta is about fifty-three point one three degrees.

blocks.problem: Solve for α: 3 sec α = 1,4.

steps.reason: The given equation.
There is no sec button on the calculator, so write sec α = 1/cos α.
Multiply both sides by cos α.
Divide both sides by 1,4 to get cos α alone.
Cosine of any angle is at most 1, so this is impossible.
Write 'no solution', not 'math error'.

blocks.speech: Worked example five. Solve for alpha: three sec alpha equals one point four. There is no sec button on the calculator, so write sec alpha as one over cos alpha. The equation becomes three over cos alpha equals one point four. Multiply both sides by cos alpha: three equals one point four cos alpha. Divide both sides by one point four: cos alpha equals three over one point four, about two point one four. But cosine of an angle can never be more than one. So there is no solution. Write no solution, not error.

question.prompt: Solve for θ: tan θ = 0,5. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
question.why: Learners press tan instead of inverse tan and get a tiny ratio instead of an angle.
question.rightWay: tan θ is already alone, so apply the inverse tangent (SHIFT tan) to 0,5 and round the calculator angle to 2 decimal places.

blocks.hint: Use the inverse tangent: SHIFT tan on most calculators.
blocks.speech: Your turn. Solve for theta: tan theta equals zero point five. Give your answer correct to two decimal places. Hint: use the inverse tangent, shift tan on most calculators.

question.prompt: Solve for θ: sin θ = 1/√2. Give the exact answer.
question.why: Learners round 0,7071 early and miss that this is the exact special ratio for 45°.
question.rightWay: 1/√2 is the exact sine of 45° from the special angles of Lesson 4, so the answer is exactly 45°.

blocks.hint: This ratio is one of the special angle values from Lesson 4.
blocks.speech: Your turn. Solve for theta: sin theta equals one over the square root of two. Give the exact answer. Hint: this ratio is one of the special angle values from Lesson four.

blocks.why: sin changes an angle into a ratio; to go back from the ratio to the angle you must use the inverse function sin⁻¹, not sin a second time.
blocks.speech: Here is a common mistake. Sin theta equals zero point five, and the learner writes theta equals sin of zero point five, which gives a tiny number near zero point zero zero nine. The right way is theta equals inverse sin of zero point five, which is thirty degrees. Why the wrong way fails: sine turns an angle into a ratio. To go from the ratio back to the angle, you need the inverse function, not sine again.

blocks.text:
Three questions decide your method. Is the angle hiding in a triangle with two known sides? Write the ratio, then apply the inverse.

Is it an equation? Isolate the ratio first, then invert. Is the ratio a special value such as 0,5, 1 or 1/√2? Then the answer is exact: 30°, 45° or 60°.

If sin or cos would need to be more than 1, write 'no solution'.
blocks.speech: Let us tie it together. Three questions decide your method. Is the angle hiding in a triangle where two sides are known? Write the ratio, then apply the inverse. Is it an equation? Isolate the ratio with algebra first, then invert. Is the ratio a special value like zero point five, one, or one over the square root of two? Then the answer is exact: thirty, forty-five or sixty degrees. And if sine or cosine would need to be more than one, there is no solution.

summary: To find an unknown angle from two sides: write sin, cos or tan θ = the ratio of the two sides, then apply sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹.
In an equation, isolate the trig ratio first (divide both sides), then apply the inverse function.
sin⁻¹ 0,5 means the angle whose sine is 0,5; it does not mean 1 divided by sin.
Exact special answers: sin θ = 1/2 gives 30°, cos θ = 1/2 gives 60°, sin θ = cos θ = 1/√2 gives 45°, tan θ = 1 gives 45°, tan θ = √3 gives 60°, tan θ = 1/√3 gives 30°.
If sin θ or cos θ would have to be more than 1, write 'no solution', not 'error'.

practice.prompt: Solve for θ: sin θ = 0,5. Give the exact answer.
practice.why: Learners sometimes press sin instead of inverse sin and get a tiny number instead of an angle.
practice.rightWay: 0,5 is the exact sine of the special angle 30°, so θ = sin⁻¹(0,5) = 30°.

practice.prompt: Solve for θ: tan θ = 1. Give the exact answer.
practice.why: Learners forget that tan 45° = 1 and reach for the calculator when the answer is exact.
practice.rightWay: 1 is the exact tangent of the special angle 45°, so θ = tan⁻¹(1) = 45°.

practice.prompt: Solve for θ: cos θ = 0,75. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
practice.why: Learners press cos instead of inverse cos, or round too early in the working.
practice.rightWay: cos θ is already alone, so apply the inverse cosine (SHIFT cos) to 0,75 and round the calculator angle to 2 decimal places.

practice.prompt: Solve for x: 3 sin x = 1,5. Give the exact answer.
practice.why: Learners apply the inverse sine before dividing by 3.
practice.rightWay: First divide both sides by 3 to get sin x = 0,5, then apply the inverse sine to get x = 30°.

practice.prompt: In a right-angled triangle, the side opposite θ is 4 and the side adjacent to θ is 7. Find θ, correct to 2 decimal places.
practice.why: Learners use sine or cosine instead of tangent when the opposite and adjacent sides are known.
practice.rightWay: Opposite and adjacent are known, so tan θ = 4/7; apply the inverse tangent and round to 29,74°.

practice.prompt: Solve for θ: tan θ = 1/√3. Give the exact answer.
practice.why: Learners round 1/√3 too early and miss the exact special angle 30°.
practice.rightWay: 1/√3 is the exact tangent of 30° from the special angles, so θ = 30° exactly.

practice.prompt: Solve for β: cos β = 1,2. Choose the correct statement.
steps: cos of an angle can never be more than 1
practice.why: Learners trust the calculator error message instead of checking that cosine cannot exceed 1.
practice.rightWay: Cosine of an angle is never more than 1, so 1,2 is impossible; the correct statement is 'no solution'.

practice.prompt: A ladder 6 m long leans against a wall. Its foot is 2,5 m from the wall. Find the angle the ladder makes with the ground, correct to 2 decimal places.
steps: Hypotenuse = 6 m (the ladder), adjacent = 2,5 m (the ground)
practice.why: Learners divide the wrong way and use 6/2,5 as the cosine ratio.
practice.rightWay: The ladder is the hypotenuse and the ground side is adjacent to the angle, so cos θ = 2,5/6; apply the inverse cosine to get θ ≈ 65,38°.

lessons.title: Angles in the Cartesian plane
objectives: You will be able to find r from a point (x;y) using r squared = x squared + y squared.
You will be able to write sin, cos and tan for an angle in standard position as y over r, x over r and y over x.
You will be able to use the signs of x and y to place an angle in the correct quadrant.

keyWords.meaning: The point O(0; 0) where the x-axis and y-axis cross.
An angle measured from the positive x-axis in an anti-clockwise direction to a line from the origin.
One of the four regions of the Cartesian plane, numbered 1 to 4 anti-clockwise starting at the top right.
The distance from the origin to a point; it is a length, so r is always positive.
A picture of the four quadrants showing which ratios are positive in each one.
An angle greater than 90 degrees but less than 180 degrees, so it lies in the second quadrant.
What tan 90 degrees is, because you cannot divide by zero.
A root like sqrt(21) that is left in exact form instead of rounded.

blocks.text:
In earlier lessons you used sin, cos and tan inside right-angled triangles. Now we take those ideas onto the Cartesian plane.

Plot any point P(x; y). Draw a line from the origin O to P, and drop a dotted line straight down to the x-axis. You have made a right-angled triangle: the horizontal leg is x, the vertical leg is y, and the line OP is the hypotenuse. We call this distance r.

The angle the line OP makes with the positive x-axis, measured anti-clockwise, is called the angle in standard position. Because the triangle only depends on the angle, the ratios work for any angle, not just angles inside a drawn triangle.
blocks.speech: So far we have used sin, cos and tan inside right-angled triangles. Now we move those ideas onto the Cartesian plane. Plot any point P with coordinates x and y. Draw a line from the origin O to P, and drop a dotted line straight down to the x-axis. That makes a right-angled triangle. The horizontal leg has length x, the vertical leg has length y, and the line from O to P is the hypotenuse, which we call r. The angle between the line OP and the positive x-axis, measured anti-clockwise, is called the angle in standard position. Because the triangle only depends on the size of the angle, these ratios work for any angle at all.

blocks.caption: The point P(2; 3) makes a right-angled triangle with the x-axis: horizontal leg 2, vertical leg 3, hypotenuse r.
blocks.speech: The picture shows the point P with coordinates two and three. A line runs from the origin to P and its length is r. A dotted line drops from P straight down to the x-axis, cutting off a horizontal leg of length two and a vertical leg of length three. The angle theta is measured from the positive x-axis anti-clockwise up to the line OP. This is the angle in standard position.

blocks.text:
With the angle marked theta, the vertical leg y is opposite theta and the horizontal leg x is next to theta, so the old definitions become:

sin theta = y/r, cos theta = x/r, tan theta = y/x.

You find r with the theorem of Pythagoras: r squared = x squared + y squared. Remember r is a length, so r is always positive, even when x or y is negative. The reciprocals work the same way: cosec theta = r/y, sec theta = r/x, cot theta = x/y.
blocks.speech: Mark the angle theta. The vertical leg y is opposite theta and the horizontal leg x is next to theta, so the definitions become: sin theta equals y over r, cos theta equals x over r, and tan theta equals y over x. You find r using the theorem of Pythagoras: r squared equals x squared plus y squared. Remember that r is a length, so r is always positive, even when x or y is negative. The reciprocals also work this way: cosec theta is r over y, sec theta is r over x, and cot theta is x over y.

blocks.problem: P is the point (3; 4) and theta is the angle between OP and the positive x-axis. Find sin theta without a calculator.

steps.reason: Read the coordinates of P; x is the horizontal leg and y is the vertical leg.
Use the theorem of Pythagoras to find r squared.
Take the positive square root, because r is a length and lengths are positive.
Substitute y and r into the definition sin theta = y over r.

blocks.speech: The problem: P is the point three; four, and theta is the angle between O P and the positive x-axis. Find sin theta without a calculator. Step one: read the coordinates, so x is three and y is four. Step two: use Pythagoras, r squared equals three squared plus four squared, which is nine plus sixteen, so r squared is twenty five. Step three: r equals five, taking the positive root because r is a length. Step four: sin theta equals y over r, which is four fifths. The answer is four fifths.

blocks.text:
The plane is divided into four quadrants, numbered anti-clockwise from the top right. In every quadrant r is positive, but the signs of x and y change, so the ratios can be positive or negative.

Quadrant 1: x and y both positive, so all ratios are positive. Quadrant 2: x negative, y positive, so only sin (and cosec) are positive. Quadrant 3: x and y both negative, so tan (and cot) are positive, because a negative over a negative is positive. Quadrant 4: x positive, y negative, so only cos (and sec) are positive.

The CAST diagram shows this: going anti-clockwise from quadrant 4, the letters C, A, S, T tell you which ratio is positive in each quadrant.
blocks.speech: The plane is divided into four quadrants, numbered anti-clockwise from the top right. In every quadrant r is positive, but the signs of x and y change, so the ratios can be positive or negative. In quadrant one, both x and y are positive, so all ratios are positive. In quadrant two, x is negative and y is positive, so only sin and cosec are positive. In quadrant three, both x and y are negative, so tan and cot are positive, because a negative divided by a negative is positive. In quadrant four, x is positive and y is negative, so only cos and sec are positive. The CAST diagram shows this: reading anti-clockwise from quadrant four, the letters C, A, S, T tell you which ratio is positive in each quadrant.

blocks.caption: The CAST diagram: the letter in each quadrant shows which ratio is positive there.
blocks.speech: This is the CAST diagram. The plane is divided into four quadrants. In the top right, quadrant one, the letter A means all ratios are positive. In the top left, quadrant two, the letter S means sin is positive there. In the bottom left, quadrant three, the letter T means tan is positive there. In the bottom right, quadrant four, the letter C means cos is positive there. Remember r is always positive; only the signs of x and y change.

blocks.problem: P(-3; 4) is a point with origin O. Theta is the angle between OP and the positive x-axis. Without a calculator, determine cos theta, 3 tan theta and (1/2) cosec theta.

steps.reason: Read the coordinates; the point is in the second quadrant, so x is negative and y is positive.
Pythagoras; squaring a negative gives a positive, and r is positive.
Substitute x and r into cos theta = x over r.
Substitute y and x into tan theta = y over x, then multiply by 3.
Cosec theta is r over y; substitute r = 5 and y = 4, then multiply by one half.

blocks.answer: cos theta = -3/5; 3 tan theta = -4; (1/2) cosec theta = 5/8
blocks.speech: The problem: P is the point minus three; four, and theta is the angle between O P and the positive x-axis. Find cos theta, three tan theta, and one half times cosec theta, without a calculator. Step one: x is minus three and y is four, so P is in the second quadrant. Step two: by Pythagoras, r squared equals nine plus sixteen, which is twenty five, so r is five. Step three: cos theta equals x over r, which is minus three fifths. Step four: tan theta is y over x, four over minus three, and three times that is minus four. Step five: cosec theta is r over y, five quarters, and half of that is five eighths. The answers are cos theta equals minus three fifths, three tan theta equals minus four, and one half cosec theta equals five eighths.

question.prompt: B is the point (1; -3) on the Cartesian plane with origin O. Beta is the angle between OB and the positive x-axis. Without a calculator, find tan beta.
question.why: Learners often forget the sign of y and write tan beta = 3 instead of -3.
question.rightWay: The point (1; -3) is in the fourth quadrant, so y is negative. tan beta = y over x = minus three over one = -3.

blocks.hint: tan beta is y over x; use the signs of the coordinates exactly as they are.
blocks.speech: Your turn. B is the point one; minus three, and beta is the angle between O B and the positive x-axis. Find tan beta without a calculator. Hint: tan beta is y over x, and you must keep the signs of the coordinates.

blocks.why: Dropping the minus sign loses the information that the point is left of the y-axis. The x-coordinate is -3, and cos theta = x/r, so the answer must be negative. Also, never make r negative to fix signs: r is a length and is always positive.
blocks.speech: A common mistake: for the point minus three; four, writing cos theta as three fifths. The right way is cos theta equals minus three fifths. Why? The x-coordinate is minus three, and cos theta is x over r, so the negative sign must be kept. Do not try to fix the sign by making r negative; r is a length and is always positive.

blocks.problem: K is the point (-5; y) in the third quadrant. OK is 13 units and theta is the angle that OK makes with the positive x-axis. Determine the value of y.

steps.reason: Read the x-coordinate and the distance from the origin.
Rearrange Pythagoras to make y squared the subject.
Substitute the known values; squaring -5 gives 25.
Take the square root; both signs are possible at this stage.
K is in the third quadrant, where y is negative, so y must be -12.

blocks.speech: The problem: K is the point minus five; y in the third quadrant, O K is thirteen units, and theta is the angle that O K makes with the positive x-axis. Find y. Step one: x is minus five and r is thirteen. Step two: rearrange Pythagoras so y squared equals r squared minus x squared. Step three: y squared equals one hundred and sixty nine minus twenty five, which is one hundred and forty four. Step four: y could be twelve or minus twelve. Step five: K is in the third quadrant, where y is negative, so y equals minus twelve. The answer is y equals minus twelve.

question.prompt: If sin theta = 0,4 and theta is an obtuse angle, determine cos theta without a calculator. Leave your answer in surd form.
steps: sin theta = 0,4 = 2/5 = y/r, so y = 2 and r = 5
x = -sqrt(21) (obtuse angle, so second quadrant, x negative)
question.why: Learners forget that an obtuse angle is in the second quadrant and give the positive root for x.
question.rightWay: An obtuse angle lies between 90 degrees and 180 degrees, in the second quadrant. There x is negative, so cos theta = minus the square root of twenty one over five.

blocks.hint: Write 0,4 as a fraction to get y and r, then use Pythagoras; remember an obtuse angle is in the second quadrant.

blocks.text:
The special angles now include 0 degrees and 90 degrees.

When theta = 0 degrees the opposite side y is 0, so sin 0 degrees = 0, cos 0 degrees = x/r = 1 and tan 0 degrees = 0.

When theta = 90 degrees the adjacent side x is 0, so sin 90 degrees = 1, cos 90 degrees = 0, but tan 90 degrees = y/0, which is undefined. You cannot divide by zero, so tan 90 degrees has no value. This is why the CAST diagram matters: the sign of a ratio follows from the signs of x and y in that quadrant.

At ninety degrees, the adjacent side x is zero, so sin ninety degrees is one and cos ninety degrees is zero. But tan ninety degrees is y over zero, which is undefined; you cannot divide by zero. This is why the CAST diagram matters: the sign of each ratio follows from the signs of x and y in that quadrant.

Then read off the signs of x and y from the quadrant and substitute into sin theta = y/r, cos theta = x/r or tan theta = y/x. When a question gives you one ratio instead of coordinates, write it as y over r, x over r or y over x to read off x, y and r, then use the quadrant to choose the correct signs.

lessons.title: Angles of elevation and depression
objectives: You will be able to identify the angle of elevation and the angle of depression in a diagram.
You will be able to draw a right-angled triangle from a word problem.
You will be able to use trigonometric ratios to find a missing length or angle in a two-dimensional problem.

keyWords.meaning: The angle measured upwards from the horizontal to the line of sight.
The angle measured downwards from the horizontal to the line of sight.
A flat level line or surface from which angles are measured.
The straight line from an observer's eye to the object being looked at.
Another name for the angle of elevation, measured from the horizontal.
The longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle.
The side of a right-angled triangle that is opposite the marked angle.
The side of a right-angled triangle next to the marked angle that is not the hypotenuse.

blocks.text:
Trigonometry is used when we know an angle and one side of a right-angled triangle, or when we must find an angle from two sides. In real problems the triangle is often hidden in a description: a building, a kite string, a ladder or a cliff.

Two special angles describe a line of sight. The angle of elevation is measured upwards from the horizontal. The angle of depression is measured downwards from the horizontal.
blocks.speech: Trigonometry is used when we know an angle and one side of a right angled triangle, or when we must find an angle from two sides. In real problems the triangle is often hidden in a description: a building, a kite string, a ladder or a cliff. Two special angles describe a line of sight. The angle of elevation is measured upwards from the horizontal. The angle of depression is measured downwards from the horizontal.

blocks.caption: The observer at A looks up to C. The angle between the horizontal AB and the line of sight AC is the angle of elevation θ.
blocks.speech: The picture shows a right angled triangle. A is the observer on level ground. B is the foot of the building. C is the top. The side A B is horizontal and the side B C is vertical, so the angle at B is ninety degrees. The angle at A, between the horizontal A B and the line of sight A C, is the angle of elevation, called theta.

blocks.text:
For an object below the observer, draw a horizontal line from the observer. The angle between this horizontal line and the line of sight downwards is the angle of depression.

The horizontal line at the top is parallel to the ground. By alternate angles, the angle of depression from the top equals the angle of elevation from the object below.
blocks.speech: For an object below the observer, draw a horizontal line from the observer. The angle between this horizontal line and the line of sight downwards is the angle of depression. The horizontal line at the top is parallel to the ground. By alternate angles, the angle of depression from the top equals the angle of elevation from the object below.

blocks.caption: The observer at P looks down to R. The angle between the horizontal PQ and the line of sight PR is the angle of depression α.
blocks.speech: The picture shows a right angled triangle. P is the observer at the top. Q is a point on the horizontal line through P. R is the object below. The side P Q is horizontal and Q R is vertical, so the angle at Q is ninety degrees. The angle at P, between the horizontal P Q and the line of sight P R, is the angle of depression, called alpha.

blocks.text:
The angle of inclination is another name for the angle of elevation. It is measured from the horizontal.

In a diagram with a top and a bottom, the depression angle from the top to the bottom and the elevation angle from the bottom to the top are equal. They are alternate angles between two parallel horizontal lines.

In a diagram with a top and a bottom, the depression angle from the top to the bottom and the elevation angle from the bottom to the top are equal. They are alternate angles between two parallel horizontal lines.

To solve a word problem: draw a sketch, mark the right angle, and draw the horizontal and vertical sides. Label the known angle, the known side and the unknown side.

The side opposite the angle is the opposite side. The side next to the angle that is not the hypotenuse is the adjacent side. The longest side, opposite the right angle, is the hypotenuse. Use sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite/adjacent.

blocks.speech: A building is fifty metres from point P on level ground. The angle of elevation from P to the top of the building is thirty two degrees. Find the height h of the building, correct to two decimal places. The height h is opposite the thirty two degree angle and fifty metres is adjacent, so use tangent. Tangent of thirty two degrees equals h over fifty. Multiply both sides by fifty. h equals fifty times tangent of thirty two degrees. blocks.speech: Mandla flies a kite on a seventeen metre string. The string makes an angle of sixty three degrees with the horizontal. Find the height h of the kite and the horizontal distance d, correct to two decimal places. The height h is opposite the sixty three degree angle and the string is the hypotenuse, so use sine. Sine of sixty three degrees equals h over seventeen. Multiply both sides by seventeen. h equals seventeen times sine of sixty three degrees. Use a calculator in degree mode. h equals fifteen comma one four seven and more, which is fifteen comma one five metres. The horizontal distance d is adjacent to the angle and the string is the hypotenuse, so use cosine. Cosine of sixty three degrees equals d over seventeen. d equals seventeen times cosine of sixty three degrees, which is seven comma seven one seven and more, so seven comma seven two metres. The height is fifteen comma one five metres and the horizontal distance is seven comma seven two metres.

Elevation and depression are not new ratios. They only tell you where to put the angle: above or below the horizontal. Once the right-angled triangle is drawn, the problem is the same as finding a side or an angle with sin, cos or tan.

Remember that the angle of elevation from below equals the angle of depression from above.

practice.prompt: An observer at B is 150 m horizontally from a cellphone tower. The angle of elevation to the top of the tower is 28° and the angle of depression to the bottom of the tower is 40°. Find the total height of the tower, correct to the nearest metre.

practice.rightWay: Total height = 150 tan 28° + 150 tan 40° ≈ 206 m.
